'''Harold Carl Otto Loesch''' (October 3, 1926 – May 12, 2011) was a [[marine biology|marine biologist]] and [[oceanography|oceanographer]] who is credited with being the first to examine the [[Mobile Bay jubilee]] in an {{nowrap|[[academic journal]]<ref name=MAY>May, E.B. 1973.  Extensive oxygen depletion in Mobile Bay, Alabama.  [[Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography|Limnology and Oceanography]] 18:353-366.</ref>}} {{nowrap|([[Ecology (journal)|''Ecology'']]).}}<sup>[https://www.jstor.org/stable/1930218 paper]</sup>

Much of his career was as an [[Academic staff|academic]] holding a [[professorship]] in the Department of Marine Sciences at [[Louisiana State University]], though he also spent many years working for the [[United Nations]] agencies [[UNESCO]] and [[FAO]] to develop  [[Fishery|fisheries]] in [[newly industrialized country|newly industrialized countries]].  His principal areas of research were [[shrimp]], [[copepods]], and commercial fisheries development.

== Academic career ==
Loesch received his [[Ph.D.]] in biological oceanography from [[Texas A&M University]] in 1962.  He served as a professor at [[Louisiana State University]] in [[Baton Rouge]], [[Louisiana]] in the Department of Zoology and Physiology in 1968 and 1969, and then as a Professor of Marine Sciences from 1969 to 1975.  During this time he studied shrimp fisheries in nearby [[Barataria Bay]] in association with the [[National Science Foundation]] [[National Sea Grant Program|Sea Grant]] Development Office.

He also held the titles of [[visiting professor]] in both the [[Organization of American States]] Marine Sciences Program in [[Guayaquil]], [[Ecuador]], and at [[The School for Field Studies]] Marine Ecology program at [[Turks and Caicos Islands|South Caicos Island]] in the [[British West Indies]].

== Work with UNESCO and FAO ==
From 1960 to 1968 Loesch worked as a shrimp [[biologist]] and fisheries officer for the [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] of the [[United Nations]] in [[Guatemala City]], [[Guatemala]], [[Guayaquil]], [[Ecuador]] and [[Tegucigalpa]], and [[La Ceiba]], [[Honduras]].

After teaching at Louisiana State University, he returned to the service of the United Nations, this time with the [[United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization]] (UNESCO).  He served as lead biologist for the [[United Nations Development Programme]] at [[Monterrey Institute of Technology and Higher Education]] and at the [[National Autonomous University of Mexico]] Marine Station in [[Ciudad del Carmen]], [[Mexico]] from 1976 to 1980.

He served once again with FAO as a [[project manager]] for a fishery development project in [[Dhaka]], [[Bangladesh]] from 1981 to 1986.

Loesch died in May 2011 in [[Pensacola, Florida]], leaving behind five children, seven grandchildren, and five great-grandchildren.
